metrics.title: Life expectancy at birth

milestones.label: Snow traces cholera to a water pump; sanitation era begins

metrics.plain_language: Global life expectancy at birth was around 30 years until the 19th century and is now above 70, with every world region having more than doubled. Vaccines, clean water and sewers, antibiotics, better nutrition from higher farm yields, and safer births account for most of the gain.
metrics.caveats: Pre-1950 world and regional values are historical reconstructions with wide uncertainty. England's parish records supply the United Kingdom series from 1543, which is this chart's longest continuous record.

metrics.title: Child mortality (share of newborns dying before age 5)

milestones.label: Jersey City begins routine chlorination of drinking water
Oral rehydration therapy declared a major advance by The Lancet

metrics.plain_language: In 1800 roughly 43 percent of children worldwide died before their fifth birthday; by 2024 the share was below 4 percent. Immunization, safe water, oral rehydration salts, antibiotics and better nutrition drove the decline, which happened first in Europe and North America and then, much faster, elsewhere after 1950.
metrics.caveats: Pre-1950 estimates for the world rely on Gapminder reconstructions; national series start when civil registration began (Sweden 1751, France 1816).

metrics.title: Maternal mortality ratio

milestones.label: Semmelweis shows handwashing cuts childbed fever
Millennium Development Goal 5 targets maternal deaths

metrics.plain_language: In 1750s Sweden about 1,000 of every 100,000 births killed the mother; in 2020 the global ratio was 212 per 100,000 and below 10 in most high-income countries. Antiseptic practice, antibiotics, safe blood transfusion and skilled attendance at birth turned this common cause of death into a rare one where they are available.
metrics.caveats: Global estimates only begin in 1985 (WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank, UN DESA); long national series come from historical registers with changing definitions. Regional entity names follow the source file.

metrics.title: Share of people living in extreme poverty

milestones.label: Haber-Bosch ammonia plant at Oppau; Ford moving assembly line

metrics.plain_language: Around 1820 roughly three quarters of humanity lived below a cost of basic needs poverty line; by 2018 that share was about 10 percent even as population grew sevenfold. Industrial productivity, mechanized farming, cheap transport and, since 1980, rapid growth in East and South Asia drove that fall.
metrics.caveats: Moatsos (2021) built this 1820 to 2018 series from basic needs costs and historical national accounts, which are uncertain before 1950. World Bank figures use a $3.00 per day line in 2021 prices and cover 1990 onward, so levels differ.

metrics.title: GDP per capita

milestones.label: World Wide Web opens to the public

metrics.plain_language: Output per person barely moved for most of the millennium: Britain produced around 1,100 to 2,400 dollars per person a year from 1000 to 1700. After 1820 it rose more than tenfold worldwide. Mechanized production and fossil energy made that break, followed by electrification and information technology.
metrics.caveats: Maddison Project estimates before 1820 exist only for some countries and rest on sparse records; the world series begins in 1820. Values are in 2011 international dollars, which abstracts from large changes in what money could buy.

metrics.title: Literacy rate
metrics.unit: % of adults able to read and write

milestones.label: Steam powered printing press at The Times

metrics.plain_language: Around 1475 fewer than one in five adults in Western Europe could read; in 1820 about 12 percent of the world could, and in 2024 about 88 percent can. Cheap printed text made literacy useful and affordable, and mass schooling made it universal.
metrics.caveats: Pre-1800 figures (Buringh and van Zanden 2009) are inferred from book production and signatures; modern figures come from censuses and UNESCO with varying definitions of literacy.

metrics.title: Annual working hours per worker

milestones.label: Ford doubles pay and later adopts the five day week
US Fair Labor Standards Act sets a 40 hour week

metrics.plain_language: Workers in the United Kingdom averaged about 2,750 hours a year in 1870 and about 1,500 in 2023, with similar declines in the United States, France and Germany. Rising productivity from mechanized and later automated production let societies take part of that gain as shorter hours, alongside labor movements and law.
metrics.caveats: No global series exists, so this main line shows the United Kingdom. Country definitions of workers and hours differ, and pre-1950 values are reconstructions by Huberman and Minns.

metrics.title: Price of light
metrics.unit: British pounds (2000 prices) per million lumen-hours, United Kingdom

milestones.label: Murdoch lights his house with coal gas
Nobel Prize for the blue LED

metrics.plain_language: In 1300 one million lumen-hours of light in Britain cost about 30,000 pounds in year 2000 money; today it costs about 2 pounds, down more than 10,000 times. Each new lighting technology, from gas and kerosene to incandescent bulbs, fluorescents and LEDs, cut prices by an order of magnitude, that is, tenfold.
metrics.caveats: Fouquet and Pearson (2006) built this United Kingdom series, extended by Our World in Data, as rolling averages across lighting sources. Nordhaus's United States estimates show similar decline.

metrics.title: Deaths from famines per decade

milestones.label: Haber-Bosch synthetic ammonia at industrial scale
Railways, trucks and food aid logistics after WWII
Borlaug's Nobel for the Green Revolution

technologies: Famine early warning and satellite monitoring
metrics.plain_language: Famines killed 16 million people in the 1870s and nearly 30 million in the 1960s. Since the 1990s they have killed fewer than 1.2 million per decade, even though world population tripled. Higher yields, transport that can move grain to where it is scarce, and early warning systems account for much of that fall; most remaining famine deaths occur in wars.
metrics.caveats: Famine death tolls are uncertain, especially for the 19th century and for China 1959 to 1961. This series counts deaths by decade of each famine and relies on Our World in Data's famine dataset.

sources.title: Our World in Data: Deaths from famines by decade

metrics.title: Deaths from natural disasters per decade
metrics.unit: deaths per decade (sum of annual EM-DAT counts)

milestones.label: Bhola cyclone kills hundreds of thousands in Bangladesh
Bangladesh begins cyclone preparedness and shelter program
Indian Ocean tsunami prompts global warning systems

technologies: Early warning systems and cyclone shelters
metrics.plain_language: During 1920 to 1939 natural disasters killed about 5 million people per decade, mostly through droughts and floods. During 2010 to 2019 they killed about 450,000, despite far larger population. Forecasting, early warning, evacuation and sturdier construction cut deaths from storms and floods; earthquakes now kill most.
metrics.caveats: EM-DAT counts are incomplete before 1960, and totals are dominated by few events. Decadal values sum reported annual deaths; 2020 to 2025 is shown as one partial decade.

metrics.title: Smallpox cases reported worldwide

milestones.label: Jenner inoculates James Phipps with cowpox

metrics.plain_language: Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in 1900 to 1999 alone. After WHO's intensified campaign began in 1966, reported cases fell from 132,000 in 1967, with one last surge of 218,000 in 1974, to zero by 1979; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. It remains humanity's only disease eliminated by technology and coordinated public health.
metrics.caveats: Reported cases greatly understate true incidence before the 1960s, when many countries had weak surveillance; the series shows reports to WHO, not estimated infections.

It remains the only human disease eliminated by technology and coordinated public health.

metrics.title: Cumulative lives saved by childhood vaccination since 1974

milestones.label: Nobel Prize to Kariko and Weissman

technologies: Measles, polio, DTP and BCG vaccines
metrics.plain_language: Modeling in The Lancet estimates that routine childhood vaccination averted 154 million deaths between 1974 and 2024. Of those, 146 million were children under five, and measles vaccine alone accounts for about 94 million. This is roughly 40 percent of the fall in infant mortality over that period.
metrics.caveats: These are model based counterfactual estimates (Shattock et al. 2024) with uncertainty intervals, and the final two years are extrapolated; COVID-19 vaccines are not included.

metrics.title: Cereal yields

milestones.label: First genetically modified food crop approved

metrics.plain_language: English wheat yields stayed near half a tonne per hectare from 1275 to 1500 and reached about 1 tonne in 1750. World cereal yields rose from 1.4 tonnes per hectare in 1961 to 4.2 in 2024. Synthetic fertilizer, bred varieties, irrigation and mechanization let food output outrun population growth on almost unchanged farmland.
metrics.caveats: FAO data begin in 1961; Broadberry et al. and Brassley reconstructed the long United Kingdom wheat series, which has gaps. Yield gains came with fertilizer runoff, pesticide harms and groundwater depletion.

metrics.title: Share of people with access to electricity

milestones.label: Renewables generate more electricity than coal

technologies: Central power stations and AC grids
metrics.plain_language: Between 1998 and 2023 the share of people with electricity rose from 73 percent to about 92 percent, with most of the remaining gap in sub-Saharan Africa. Grid expansion in Asia and, more recently, cheap solar panels and batteries for off-grid homes drove that gain.
metrics.caveats: World Bank data begin after 1990 and record whether households are connected, not whether supply is reliable. United States and European access rose from near zero in 1880 to near universal by the 1950s, before this series starts.

metrics.title: Share of people using safely managed drinking water

milestones.label: Paisley, Scotland installs the first municipal sand filter
John Snow's Broad Street pump investigation
Continuous chlorination of a public supply in Jersey City

metrics.plain_language: Between 2000 and 2024 the share of people with safely managed drinking water rose from 61 to about 74 percent. More than 90 percent now have at least basic service. Filtration, chlorination and piped networks ended waterborne epidemics that killed millions in 19th century cities, and they remain the main lever today.
metrics.caveats: WHO/UNICEF monitoring of safely managed water only begins in 2000; earlier history is documented for individual cities rather than as a global series.

metrics.title: Cost of a 3-minute New York to London call

milestones.label: Transatlantic radiotelephone service opens at $75 for 3 minutes
Telstar relays live television across the Atlantic
TAT-8, first transatlantic fiber optic cable

metrics.plain_language: When transatlantic telephone service opened in 1927, one three minute call cost 75 dollars, about 244 dollars in 1990 money for 1930. By 1990 that call cost about 3 dollars, and by 2004 the index had fallen to one thousandth of its 1930 level. Cables, satellites, fiber optics and finally internet telephony made long-distance calls nearly free.
metrics.caveats: OECD's index tracks standard tariffs for one three minute call and stops in 2004, before internet calls made that price effectively zero. Air and sea indices are shown for comparison.

metrics.title: Time to cross the Atlantic
metrics.world_series_label: North Atlantic crossing, Europe to New York

milestones.label: Lindbergh flies New York to Paris

metrics.plain_language: Crossing the Atlantic took the Mayflower 66 days in 1620, steamships 15 days in 1838, ocean liners 4.5 days in 1907 and jets about 7 hours since the 1960s. Steam, then internal combustion and jet engines, cut that journey by more than 200 times; speed has plateaued since Concorde retired in 2003.
metrics.caveats: Points are notable crossings, not annual averages. Sailing times varied widely with winds, and both jet era points show midpoints of stated 6.5 to 8 hour ranges.

metrics.title: World population
metrics.plain_language: World population grew from about 320 million in year 1000 to 1 billion around 1804 and 8 billion in 2022. Falling death rates from better food, sanitation and medicine drove that growth; development plus contraception has since cut birth rates, so growth is slowing.
metrics.caveats: Estimates before 1800 are reconstructions (HYDE) with wide ranges; Up is drawn as the better direction for display only; population growth is not simply good or bad.

metrics.title: Share of children in child labor
metrics.unit: % of children aged 5 to 17 (ILO global estimates)

milestones.label: British Factory Act limits child work in textile mills
US Fair Labor Standards Act bans most child labor
ILO Convention 182 on the worst forms of child labour

metrics.plain_language: In 1851 about 28 percent of English children were recorded as working. In 2000, 16 percent of children worldwide aged 5 to 17 were in child labor; by 2024 that share was 7.8 percent, or 138 million children. Rising incomes from productive technology, schooling and law reduced it, though progress stalled between 2016 and 2020.
metrics.caveats: Definitions differ across series. Historical census shares, ILO counts of economically active children aged 10 to 14 (1950 to 1995) and ILO child labor aged 5 to 17 (2000 onward) are not directly comparable.

metrics.title: Death rate from infectious diseases
metrics.world_series_label: United States, crude infectious disease mortality (Armstrong et al. 1999)
metrics.plain_language: In the United States infectious diseases killed 797 of every 100,000 people in 1900, 75 in 1952 and 36 in 1980. HIV then pushed that rate back up to 63 in 1995. Most of this decline came before antibiotics, from clean water, pasteurized milk and sanitation; the 1938 to 1952 drop of 8 percent per year coincided with sulfa drugs, penicillin and streptomycin.
metrics.caveats: No consistent global series exists before 1990. This main line is United States crude mortality from Armstrong, Conn and Pinner (JAMA 1999); WHO Mortality Database series are age-standardized and cover only infectious and parasitic causes, so levels are not comparable across series.

metrics.title: Cost to sequence a human genome

milestones.label: Next generation sequencers break Moore's law trend

metrics.plain_language: Sequencing one human genome cost about 95 million dollars in 2001 and about 525 dollars in 2022. That decline is far steeper than Moore's law, which describes computing costs halving roughly every two years, and it followed short read sequencers in 2008. Cheap sequencing underlies cancer genomics, rapid pathogen tracking and newborn screening.
metrics.caveats: NHGRI figures are production cost estimates for its own sequencing centers, not retail prices. Its public table ends in May 2022, so later vendor claims of 100 to 200 dollar genomes are not included.

metrics.title: Price of solar photovoltaic modules

milestones.label: Renewables overtake coal in electricity generation

metrics.plain_language: One watt of solar module capacity cost about 130 dollars in 1975 and about 0.27 dollars in 2024 in constant prices, down roughly 99.8 percent. Each doubling of cumulative production has cut prices by around 20 percent, making solar the cheapest new electricity in most of the world.
metrics.caveats: Inflation adjusted. Module prices exclude installation, land and storage.

metrics.title: Lithium-ion battery pack price
metrics.unit: US$ per kWh (as reported each survey year)

milestones.label: BYD becomes the largest EV maker

metrics.plain_language: BloombergNEF's survey shows average lithium-ion pack prices falling from 176 dollars per kWh in 2018 to 108 dollars in 2025. BNEF earlier reported an 85 percent fall between 2010 and 2018. Cheaper batteries put electric cars near price parity with gasoline cars and make solar power usable after dark.
metrics.caveats: Volume-weighted average across end uses, as reported in each year's release (not restated to a common inflation-adjusted base; BNEF later restated 2024 as $118 in 2025 dollars). The full historical series cannot be redistributed.

shadows.title: Annual CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and industry
shadows.unit: billion tonnes of CO2 per year
shadows.plain_language: Fossil CO2 emissions were near zero in 1750, about 2 billion tonnes in 1900 and about 38.6 billion tonnes in 2024. Combustion technologies that raised incomes and life expectancy are also warming the climate, and emissions have not yet begun any sustained global decline.
shadows.caveats: Excludes land use change emissions; national series are territorial, not consumption based.

shadows.title: Deaths from road injuries

milestones.label: Volvo introduces the three point seat belt
US National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act
First fatal crash on Tesla Autopilot

shadows.plain_language: Road crashes kill about 1.16 million people a year, with more than 90 percent of deaths in low and middle income countries. Worldwide, deaths per 100,000 people fell from 19 in 2000 to about 15 in 2021. Cars brought mobility and a new mass cause of death; safety engineering has cut rates mainly in rich countries so far.
shadows.caveats: WHO Global Health Estimates begin in 2000. United States counts show how deaths rose with motorization, from 36 in 1900 to more than 50,000 a year in the 1970s, before safety technology and regulation cut that rate.

shadows.title: Share of adults who are obese

milestones.label: High fructose corn syrup process commercialized

technologies: Industrial food processing and cheap calories
shadows.plain_language: Adults who are obese, meaning body mass index over 30, rose from about 5 percent in 1980 to about 16 percent in 2024, with the United States above 40 percent. Abundant cheap processed food, motorized transport and sedentary work, all products of technological progress, drove that rise.
shadows.caveats: WHO estimates are crude (not age-standardized) and modeled from surveys; BMI thresholds are an imperfect measure of health risk.

shadows.title: Daily time spent online
shadows.unit: hours per day per internet user
shadows.world_series_label: World, internet users aged 16 to 64 (GWI via DataReportal)

milestones.label: Pew: 45 percent of US teens online almost constantly
US Surgeon General advisory on social media and youth
Australia bans social media for under 16s

shadows.plain_language: Internet users worldwide spend about 6 hours 38 minutes a day online, flat since 2019 after rising sharply with smartphones. US adults went from 2.7 hours of digital media a day in 2008 to 6.3 in 2018, almost all of that increase on mobile. Technology now competes for that time, with contested effects on sleep, mood and attention.
shadows.caveats: Survey based time use is self reported and the two series use different populations and definitions; global series only exists from the late 2010s.

shadows.title: Nuclear warheads in global stockpiles
shadows.plain_language: Stockpiles grew from 6 warheads in 1945 to their peak above 70,000 in 1986 and have fallen to about 12,000, still enough to end civilization. Physics that gave humanity nuclear power also created standing existential risk, meaning threat to humanity's survival, which treaties have reduced but not removed.
shadows.caveats: Figures are Federation of American Scientists estimates; governments do not publish exact counts and retired but intact warheads are counted differently across sources.

shadows.title: Electronic waste generated

milestones.label: iPhone and the annual upgrade cycle
EU common charger rule takes effect

shadows.plain_language: In 2022 the world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste, discarded electronics, up 82 percent from 2010; only 22 percent was documented as collected and recycled. Cheap, short lived electronics came with falling computing costs, and this waste stream is growing at five times the rate of recycling.
shadows.caveats: Estimates come from UN Global E-waste Monitor reports; its 2010 value is derived from stated 82 percent growth, and its 2030 value is one projection.
